title: Scanning Electron Microscopy and the Study of Technological Styles
content: The concept of style has been of great importance for archaeological research. Originally based on formal and decorative features of objects, it has served to develop chronologies and establish cultural affiliations of archaeological finds. However, various studies have shown that observations with the naked eye can be misleading, since very similar but different styles can be confused, and there has also been the case of the imitation of certain styles, by societies that are culturally and chronologically different. This has led to the application of archaeometric techniques to establish, with greater certainty, aspects such as the origin of the raw materials. Knowledge of production techniques has also been used for the study of technological styles. This concept is based on the fact that producers have to make a series of decisions in the different steps that make up the production chain of any object: How are they going to do it and with what? These decisions can be conditioned by factors such as the environment, although historical and cultural aspects are of great importance. That is why the technological style can be a good marker of ethnicity. This paper will show the importance of the use of Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) for the study of technological styles, particularly in the archaeological shell materials of pre-Hispanic Mesoamerica [1].
